text: Every decision this chapter covered — chunk size, re-ranking, multi-query, HyDE, a knowledge graph — was a trade-off to tune, not a fact to accept. Tuning requires measuring. Eyeballing a handful of answers doesn't scale past a demo.

A RAG pipeline fails in four distinguishable ways. Context precision — of what was retrieved, how much was relevant. Context recall — of what should have been retrieved, how much actually was. Faithfulness — does the answer stick to what the context actually says. Answer relevancy — does the answer actually address the question asked. A pipeline with great retrieval and a hallucinating model needs a different fix than one with a faithful model working from bad retrieval.

Here's a real evaluation using Ragas, a widely used open-source library built for this. Each test case needs the question, what was actually retrieved, what was actually answered, and a known-good reference answer. Evaluate returns a score per metric — in this case faithfulness and context recall — run across the whole test set.

A trustworthy test set isn't a handful of easy questions — it needs real questions a user would actually ask, including ones where the honest answer is "I don't know," so the evaluation also measures whether the pipeline abstains correctly. A test set built only from questions the pipeline already handles well will always report good scores, whether or not that's true in production.
That closes out Chapter 5's advanced patterns. Chapter 6 is the capstone — building, evaluating, and presenting a complete, production-shaped RAG assistant using everything from this course.
